name: Haiti's gang war (Viv Ansanm versus the state and the Gang Suppression Force)
started: 2024-02-29 (formation of the Viv Ansanm gang coalition)
summary: Haiti's armed gangs, united since 2024 in the Viv Ansanm coalition, control most of Port-au-Prince and are expanding into the Artibonite and Centre departments. More than 5,915 people were killed in 2025 and over 3,000 in the first half of 2026, many of them in government operations using explosive drones with help from a US private military company. A UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force began deploying in April 2026, and nearly 1.5 million Haitians are displaced.

sides.name: Haitian state and allied forces
members: Haitian National Police, including a task force using explosive and FPV drones
Vectus Global (US private military company led by Erik Prince, supporting drone operations)
Gang Suppression Force (UN-authorized, successor to the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission)
backers: United States (funding pledges of about 300 million US dollars and terrorist designation of gangs)
Chad, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Guatemala, El Salvador, Jamaica, Bahamas, Belize (troop and police contributors)
leaders: Maj. Gen. Erdenebat Batsuuri (Mongolia), GSF force commander since Apr 2026
Brig. E. C. Clarke (Jamaica Defence Force), GSF deputy commander since Jun 2026
sides.strength: GSF authorized at 5,500; about 1,441 non-Chadian personnel listed plus an initial 400 Chadian troops from 1 Apr 2026, with about 1,500 Chadians expected (Wikipedia, Gang Suppression Force, Oct 2026)

sides.name: Viv Ansanm gang coalition
sides.strength: 12,000 to 20,000 members, controlling about 80 percent of metropolitan Port-au-Prince (Wikipedia, Viv Ansanm, 2026 estimate)

sides.name: Self-defence groups
members: Neighbourhood vigilante groups and the 'Bwa Kalé' movement
sides.strength: Unknown; responsible for about 4 to 6 percent of casualties (BINUH)

background: Haiti's state has been weakening for years. On 29 February 2024 rival gang federations G9 and G-Pèp joined forces as Viv Ansanm ('Living Together') and went on to take control of most of the capital. A Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission, authorized by the UN in 2023, arrived in 2024 but lacked troops, money and equipment.

In 2025 the government turned to explosive drones operated with the help of Vectus Global, a firm led by Blackwater founder Erik Prince, and the US designated Viv Ansanm a terrorist organization. In late 2025 the UN Security Council (Resolution 2793) replaced the Kenyan mission with a larger Gang Suppression Force of up to 5,500 personnel. These choices matter because they shape who is doing the killing: in some quarters most of the dead were killed in state operations rather than by gangs.
year: In the last quarter of 2025 the UN recorded 1,523 killings, bringing 2025 to more than 5,915. Drone use nearly doubled between November 2025 and January 2026; Human Rights Watch counted 1,243 people killed by drones between March 2025 and January 2026, including 17 children. On 14 January 2026 FPV drones destroyed three homes belonging to gang leader Jimmy Chérizier, who survived. In the first quarter of 2026, 1,642 people were killed, more than 69 percent of casualties occurring during security operations. Police retook the Carrefour Aéroport area in February, but gangs struck back in the countryside: on 29 to 31 March they attacked 16 localities around the capital and in Lower Artibonite, killing at least 83, and Gran Grif attacks in Artibonite killed at least 70 more.

The first 400 Chadian troops of the Gang Suppression Force arrived on 1 April 2026 as Kenyan police withdrew. In the second quarter, 1,408 people were killed; this time gangs caused 55 percent of casualties, with clashes between rival gangs in Cité Soleil and the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac killing 463 people and displacing more than 18,000. Gangs carried out their first raids in Séguin, in the South-East. In September the IOM counted nearly 1.5 million displaced. Sri Lankan and Bangladeshi contingents began arriving in October 2026, and on 18 October gangs destroyed a GSF armoured vehicle with explosives in Croix-des-Bouquets and took four Salvadoran air force technicians hostage.
situation: As of late October 2026 Viv Ansanm still controls most of Port-au-Prince and is pushing into Artibonite, Centre and the hills south of the capital, while drone strikes and police operations have contained it in parts of downtown, Delmas and Tabarre. The Gang Suppression Force is still building up toward its 5,500 ceiling and suffered its first major ambush on 18 October, when four Salvadoran airmen went missing in Croix-des-Bouquets; El Salvador said on 28 October it would send more than 2,000 soldiers to find them and fight gangs, without saying whether they will serve under the GSF. The same day the electoral council postponed the first national elections in a decade from 13 December 2026 to 18 July 2027. The GSF's initial mandate ran to the end of September 2026 and it asked for an extension to September 2028; whether and how it was renewed was not confirmed in the sources consulted.
technical: Explosive drones: HRW counts 1,243 killed and 738 injured by drone strikes between Mar 2025 and 21 Jan 2026, including 60 civilians (17 children); operations nearly doubled from Nov 2025 to Jan 2026 (Reuters via Chronicle.lu).

Drone operators: Haitian security forces with support from Vectus Global, a US private military company led by Erik Prince; the UN human rights chief called the strikes disproportionate and likely unlawful in Oct 2025.
FPV drones were used on 14 Jan 2026 to destroy three homes of Viv Ansanm leader Jimmy Chérizier (Wikipedia, Viv Ansanm).
Share of casualties caused by security operations: over 62 percent in Q4 2025, over 69 percent in Q1 2026, over 40 percent in Q2 2026 (BINUH quarterly reports).
Drone civilian harm in Q1 2026: 69 civilians among drone victims, including 5 children; two girls aged 7 and 9 badly injured when a drone fell in a courtyard in Martissant (BINUH).

GSF composition (Oct 2026): Sri Lanka 1,132, Guatemala 150 military police, El Salvador 78 air force personnel, Bangladesh 50, Jamaica 23, Bahamas 6, Belize 2, plus Chad (400 from 1 Apr 2026, about 1,500 expected); Kenyan police withdrawn (Wikipedia, Gang Suppression Force).
Chadian troops trained in the US before deploying and are based at the Vertières military base of the Haitian army (NTV Kenya/Reuters; Wikipedia).
GSF ambush, 18 Oct 2026: gangs destroyed an armoured vehicle with explosives in Croix-des-Bouquets and seized four Salvadoran air force technicians.
Viv Ansanm strength: 12,000 to 20,000 members, controlling about 80 percent of metropolitan Port-au-Prince (Wikipedia, 2026 estimate).
Gang sexual violence: at least 796 rape victims in Q2 2026, 87 percent subjected to gang rape (BINUH).
Kidnappings: at least 81 in Q2 2026, up from 57 in Q1 (BINUH).
Police abuses: more than 222 people believed killed in summary executions involving police in 2025 (BINUH Q4 2025).
Funding gap: the predecessor mission received 85 million US dollars against an estimated annual need of 600 million (Wikipedia, Gang Suppression Force).
casualties: 2025: more than 5,915 killed and 2,708 injured (BINUH, 30 Jan 2026). Q1 2026: at least 1,642 killed and 745 injured (BINUH, 8 May 2026). Q2 2026: at least 1,408 killed and 656 injured (BINUH, 25 Aug 2026). That is at least 3,050 killed in the first half of 2026. Drone strikes: 1,243 killed, Mar 2025 to Jan 2026 (Human Rights Watch, 10 Mar 2026). UN figures are minimums based on verified cases.
displaced: Nearly 1.5 million internally displaced, about 80 percent outside Port-au-Prince, with the sharpest recent rise in Artibonite (IOM via Reuters, 25 Sep 2026); more than 18,000 fled Cité Soleil and Plaine du Cul-de-Sac clashes in Q2 2026 (BINUH); more than 4,000 displaced by attacks in Kenscoff (IOM via Reuters).

timeline.event: Rival gang federations G9 and G-Pèp form the Viv Ansanm coalition.
FPV drones destroy three homes of gang leader Jimmy Chérizier.
UN reports more than 5,915 people killed in Haiti during 2025.
Human Rights Watch reports 1,243 people killed by drone strikes since March 2025.
Gangs attack 16 localities on the capital's outskirts and in Lower Artibonite over three days, killing at least 83.
First 400 Chadian troops of the Gang Suppression Force arrive.
UN reports 1,408 killed in Apr to Jun 2026, including 463 in Cité Soleil and Plaine du Cul-de-Sac clashes.
Gangs destroy a GSF armoured vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets and take four Salvadoran airmen hostage.
El Salvador pledges more than 2,000 troops; elections postponed to 18 July 2027.

outlook: Watch whether the GSF reaches strength and moves from defending fixed sites to clearing gang strongholds, the fate of the Salvadoran hostages, the renewal and funding of the GSF mandate, the civilian toll of drone strikes, and further gang expansion into Artibonite, Centre and the South-East.

zones.name: Port-au-Prince metropolitan area
zones.note: About 80 percent under Viv Ansanm control; drone strikes and police operations in downtown, Delmas and Tabarre.

zones.name: Cité Soleil and Plaine du Cul-de-Sac
zones.note: Rival gang clashes killed 463 people in Apr to Jun 2026; GSF ambush at Croix-des-Bouquets in Oct 2026.

zones.name: Kenscoff and the southern hills
zones.note: Gang push into the hills above the capital; more than 4,000 displaced.

zones.name: Artibonite department
zones.note: Gran Grif and allied gangs attack towns and farms; the fastest-growing displacement.

zones.name: Centre department (Mirebalais, Saut-d'Eau)
zones.note: Gangs keep a foothold after storming Mirebalais in 2025.

zones.name: South-East (Séguin)
zones.note: First armed gang raids recorded in Q2 2026.

battles.name: Ambush of the Gang Suppression Force at Croix-des-Bouquets
battles.outcome: GSF armoured vehicle destroyed with explosives; four Salvadoran air force technicians taken hostage. About a week later an NGO handed over four bodies that were not the hostages, including a Chadian GSF soldier and a child.
battles.forces: Gangs using explosives against an armoured vehicle; GSF patrol including Salvadoran personnel.
battles.losses: 1 armoured vehicle destroyed; 4 taken hostage; a Chadian GSF soldier among bodies later handed over (Wikipedia, Gang Suppression Force).
battles.significance: The most serious blow yet to the new UN-authorized force, just as Sri Lankan and Bangladeshi contingents arrived.

battles.name: Gang war in Cité Soleil and the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac
battles.place: Cité Soleil and Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, Port-au-Prince area, Haiti
sides: Rival gangs within and around Viv Ansanm
battles.outcome: Highest level of violence documented in these areas since at least early 2024; all services suspended. Dates cover the reporting quarter.
battles.forces: Rival gangs competing for territory and illicit revenue, using arson and sexual violence to displace residents.
battles.losses: 463 killed, 256 injured, at least 176 rape victims; more than 18,000 displaced (BINUH Q2 2026 report, 25 Aug 2026).
battles.significance: Shows that as state drone operations pressed gangs in central districts, fighting between gangs became the main killer in Q2 2026.

sources.label: BINUH: Quarterly human rights report Q2 2026

battles.name: Gang raids on the capital's outskirts and Lower Artibonite
battles.place: 16 localities on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince and in Lower Artibonite, Haiti
battles.outcome: Gangs attacked 16 localities over three days; marker approximate for the Lower Artibonite area.
battles.forces: Gang raiding parties; no state force engagement described.
battles.losses: At least 83 residents killed and 38 injured (BINUH Q1 2026 report, 8 May 2026).
battles.significance: Part of a shift of gang violence from the capital into the countryside, which is now where most displaced Haitians live.

sources.label: BINUH: Quarterly human rights report Q1 2026

battles.name: FPV drone strike on Jimmy Chérizier's homes
battles.place: Port-au-Prince, Haiti (exact neighbourhood not given in sources)
battles.outcome: Three houses belonging to Chérizier destroyed; he survived. Marker approximate.
battles.losses: No casualty figures reported (Wikipedia, Viv Ansanm).
battles.significance: A targeted drone attack on the coalition's best-known leader, part of a drone campaign that killed over 1,200 people by January 2026 according to Human Rights Watch.
